Swallow
SWOL-oh
v.t. (to take down the throat; to engulf, consume utterly; rendering Hebrew bala, Greek katapino)
Old English swelgan, to swallow. The Hebrew bala is the word for the earth opening on Korah and for the sea covering Pharaoh — and Isaiah takes that terrible verb and turns it against death itself.

Biblical Definition

To swallow up in Scripture is to engulf and abolish, and the verb has a career that runs from judgment to gospel. It first belongs to the earth: at Korah's rebellion Moses stakes his commission on a sign, that the ground should “open her mouth, and swallow them up” (Numbers 16:30) — the same verb Exodus uses of the sea swallowing Pharaoh's host. Then Isaiah performs the great reversal. The devourer becomes the devoured: “He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces” (Isaiah 25:8). Death, which has swallowed every generation, is itself taken down. Paul quotes it at the climax of the resurrection chapter, where the tense has moved from promise to accomplished fact: “then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54), and he writes elsewhere of the believer's longing “that mortality might be swallowed up of life” (2 Corinthians 5:4) — not that the body should be shed but that it should be so overwhelmed by life that death has nothing left to take. The Lord Jesus uses the word for a different and unforgettable purpose, describing scrupulous men who filter their drink and miss the point entirely: “Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel” (Matthew 23:24) — meticulous about the smallest unclean thing, and ingesting the largest.

Webster 1828 Definition

To engulf utterly. The earth swallows Korah and the sea swallows Pharaoh; then Isaiah reverses the verb — God swallows up death in victory, quoted by Paul at the resurrection; and Christ mocks the guides who strain a gnat and swallow a camel.

expand to see more

SWALLOW, v.t. [Sax. swelgan.] To take into the stomach; to receive through the gullet or esophagus into the stomach; as, to swallow food or drink.

2. To absorb; to draw and sink into an abyss or gulf; to ingulf; usually followed by up. The earth opened and swallowed them up. Num. 16.

3. To seize and waste; to exhaust; to consume.

4. To receive or embrace, as opinions or belief, without examination or scruple; to receive implicitly.

5. To occupy; to employ. Swallowed up in victory. 1 Cor. 15.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 25:8 — "He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces; and the rebuke of his people shall he take away from off all the earth: for the LORD hath spoken it."

1 Corinthians 15:54 — "So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory."

2 Corinthians 5:4 — "For we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life."

Matthew 23:24 — "Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel."

Modern Corruption

“Death is swallowed up in victory” is read at funerals as a statement that death is natural and harmless — the opposite of Paul's meaning, in which death is an enemy destroyed by an act of God, not a friend accepted.

expand to see more

Modern funeral rhetoric works hard to domesticate death: it is a part of life, a natural transition, a return to the cycle of things. Paul's language forbids it. Death in 1 Corinthians 15 is the last enemy that shall be destroyed (v. 26), it has a sting, and the sting is sin, and the strength of sin is the law. The verse quoted at gravesides is a battle report, not a reconciliation with mortality. That is why the Christian is permitted to grieve — Jesus wept at a tomb He was about to open — while grieving differently from those who have no hope. A comfort that requires pretending death is not an enemy will fail exactly when it is needed. The comfort Paul offers requires no pretending at all: the enemy is real, and it has been swallowed.

The other misuse is subtler and belongs to the over-realised eschatology that treats the victory as already complete in the believer's experience. Paul is careful with his tenses: the saying is brought to pass when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, at the last trump. Until then Christians die, and 2 Corinthians 5:4 has them groaning and burdened. A teaching that promises the swallowing-up of mortality now — freedom from sickness and infirmity as a present right — contradicts the apostle who left Trophimus at Miletum sick. And Matthew 23:24 supplies the standing warning against the scrupulosity that so often accompanies these systems: it is entirely possible to be exacting about small things while swallowing something enormous.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bala (to swallow down, engulf); Greek katapino (to drink down, swallow up) and diulizo (to strain through a filter, the verb behind strain at a gnat).

expand to see more

Hebrew bala (H1104) — to swallow, engulf; used of the earth at Korah (Numbers 16:30), the sea at the Red Sea (Exodus 15:12), and death in Isaiah 25:8.

Hebrew netsach (H5331) — victory, perpetuity; the noun in Isaiah 25:8 rendered victory.

Greek katapino (G2666) — to drink down, swallow up; used in 1 Corinthians 15:54, 2 Corinthians 5:4, and of the whale in Jonah's account.

Greek diulizo (G1368) — to strain through, filter out; the verb in Matthew 23:24, rendered strain at in the KJV.

Greek nikos (G3534) — victory; the word Paul uses three times in 1 Corinthians 15:54-57.

Usage

"“He will swallow up death in victory” — the devourer devoured; the verb of Korah and Pharaoh turned against death."

"“That mortality might be swallowed up of life” — not the shedding of the body but its overwhelming by life."

"“Strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel” — scrupulous in the trivial, indiscriminate in the enormous."
